strengths: Introduces EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, a well-motivated reformulation of a large, established egocentric action dataset into a multiple-choice QA format with model-generated hard distractors, addressing a real gap: existing video benchmarks with random or crowd-sourced distractors overestimate MLLM visual competence.

The finding that MLLMs (including GPT-4o) degrade sharply on hard, model-generated distractors (e.g., GPT-4o dropping from 87.6 to 52.2) is convincing and clearly demonstrated with both quantitative (Table 1) and qualitative evidence.

Comprehensive empirical study: systematic comparison of distractor sources (random vs. AVION vs. TIM), prompt perspective (egocentric vs. allocentric), and a full set of training techniques with both incremental (Table 3) and leave-one-out ablations (Table 7).

Strong final results: surpasses GPT-4o on the proposed benchmark (73.4-74.1 vs. 52.2 with comparable frames) and achieves SOTA on the original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action classification validation set (58.3 with official keys, 63.2 with narrations), plus consistent improvements over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline on six additional action-related benchmarks.

Thoughtful experimental design details, e.g., training with AVION distractors and evaluating on TIM distractors to create an IID/OOD split, shuffling answer positions to prevent memorization, and using multiple models (0.5B/7B) to show generality.

Good transparency: discusses negative results (GPT-4o distillation hurting performance, failed alternative approaches in Appendix 14), licensing information, released code/models, and acknowledges limitations such as K-scaling for narrations.
weaknesses: Novelty of the individual technical contributions is limited; vision token supervision, temporal detection auxiliary tasks, prior-action conditioning, and adversarial distractor training are each relatively straightforward combinations of known ideas, and the final system is essentially a stack of incremental tricks rather than a principled new method.

The benchmark is tightly coupled to one specific action recognition model (TIM) for distractor generation; the hardness and even validity of EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA depend on TIM's error modes, and potential biases inherited from TIM (e.g., its own confusions becoming 'ground-truth-defining' distractor structure) are not deeply analyzed.
Evaluation is confined to the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 validation set; no results on the held-out test/challenge server are reported, which weakens claims of state-of-the-art on the original dataset.

Improvements on the additional benchmarks (Table 5) are small (+0.4 to +2.5 points, with a -0.4 regression on NextQA), and the paper does not provide statistical significance or multiple seeds, so the generality claims rest on modest margins.

Prior-action experiments use ground-truth previous actions during training and only n=2 prior actions; the practical deployment scenario (where priors come from the model's own predictions) is touched on via test-time augmentation but not thoroughly studied.

Baseline coverage is narrow: only LLaVA-family models are fine-tuned; it is unclear whether the proposed techniques transfer to other MLLM architectures (e.g., VideoLLaMA, Qwen2-VL-based video models), limiting the generality of the recommendations.

Some evaluation fairness concerns: closed-source models are restricted to 8 frames for cost reasons, which may disadvantage them relative to the fine-tuned open models using 16-32 frames; the claim of 'outperforming GPT-4o by 21 points' should be interpreted with this framing in mind.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and interesting problem: MLLMs perform well on easy multi-choice video benchmarks but degrade sharply on hard distractors, and the reformulation of EPIC-KITCHENS-100 into a video MQA benchmark with model-generated hard negatives is a useful evaluation resource.

Comprehensive empirical study: multiple baseline models (GPT-4o, LLaVA-Video/OV variants), multiple distractor sources (random, AVION, TIM), progressive ablations (Table 3), leave-one-out ablation (Table 7), and per-class verb/noun breakdowns, which support the claims reasonably well.
The observation that official 'compressed' action keys hurt MLLM performance compared to raw narrations (Table 8, Appendix Figure 4) is an interesting and useful finding for the community.

Solid breadth of evaluation: besides EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA and EPIC-KITCHENS-100, results on EgoSchema, MVBench, VideoMME, LongVideoBench, NextQA, and PerceptionTest, with detailed sub-category tables in the appendix.
Code, models, and benchmark details (prompts, licenses) are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the contribution is largely a collection of incremental engineering tricks (egocentric prompt wording, shuffled answers, extra classification heads on vision tokens, timestamp prediction as auxiliary task, prior actions as context, test-time augmentation with a memory buffer). Each yields small gains (0.5–4 points) and the combination reads as empirical tuning rather than a principled method with insight into why it works.

Circularity and potential bias in the benchmark: the benchmark's difficulty and the test set are defined by TIM's predictions, and training uses AVION-generated distractors while evaluation uses TIM's; the headline EPIC-KITCHENS-100 'SOTA' also relies on TIM's top-20 predictions as candidates at test time. This entangles the MLLM's improvement with the specialist models it is compared against, weakening the fairness and generality of the SOTA claim (63.2 vs. TIM's 56.4 is a modest margin, achieved on the validation set only, not the challenge test set).

The comparison with GPT-4o is constrained: GPT-4o is evaluated only with 8 frames due to cost, while the proposed model uses 16–32 frames, and the claim of 'outperforming GPT-4o by 21 points' depends on this frame mismatch (the authors acknowledge the 8-vs-8 caveat only in a footnote).

Cross-benchmark generalization evidence is weak: improvements over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline on other benchmarks are small (+0.4 to +2.5) with one negative result (NextQA, -0.4), and sub-category tables show many regressions, so the 'wider applicability' claim is not strongly supported.

The training recipe introduces many design choices without ablation or justification (e.g., the 70/30 MQA split with/without prior context, n=2 prior actions, K=5 distractors, fixed padding delta=3s), making it hard to know which components are essential or how sensitive results are.
Prior-action memory at test time using model predictions plus a memory buffer is an ad hoc inference-time procedure that complicates fair comparison with baselines.
The overall pipeline is complex and the paper sometimes reads as a system report; the significance of the benchmark beyond EPIC-KITCHENS-style egocentric kitchen videos is unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether MLLMs can truly recognize fine-grained human actions, and provides evidence that current MLLMs (including GPT-4o) struggle when distractors are hard rather than trivial.

The reformulation of EPIC-KITCHENS-100 into a multiple-choice QA benchmark (EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA) using SOTA action recognition models (TIM/AVION) to mine hard distractors is a sensible, scalable benchmark design, and the paper is careful about IID vs OOD distractor settings and about avoiding position/answer memorization.

The paper reports a comprehensive set of comparisons (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaVA variants) and a systematic, incremental ablation of each proposed component (adversarial distractors, egocentric prompts, vision token supervision, temporal detection, GPT-4o distillation, direct prediction, prior-action memory), plus leave-one-out ablations in the appendix.

Evaluation goes beyond the proposed benchmark: SOTA on the original EPIC-KITCHENS-100 validation set and consistent improvements on six additional action-related benchmarks (EgoSchema, MVBench, VideoMME, LongVideoBench, NextQA, PerceptionTest), supporting the claim of broader applicability.

Discussion of language bias in the official EPIC-KITCHENS keys vs. raw narrations (Table 8, Figure 4) is an interesting and useful observation for the community, and code/model release plus detailed prompts in the appendix support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: most components are straightforward engineering additions to LLaVA-Video (shuffled adversarial distractors, extra classification heads on vision tokens, timestamp prediction, conditioning on prior actions, distillation). Individual techniques are incremental and largely validated empirically rather than via new insight.

The headline 'outperforms GPT-4o by 21 points' is on the authors' own benchmark, and GPT-4o comparisons are limited to 8 frames due to cost (footnote 1), while fine-tuned models use 16-32 frames; frame-count asymmetry makes the closed-vs-open-source comparison somewhat unfair and weakens the significance claim.

Several benchmark-design choices are selected post hoc based on how hard they are for evaluated MLLMs (e.g., choosing TIM over AVION as the distractor generator because it produced the hardest distractors), which risks tuning the benchmark to the models being evaluated; more independent justification would strengthen the design.
Improvements on the external benchmarks (Table 5) are small (+0.4 to +2.5) and inconsistent (NextQA is -0.4), so the generalization claim, while supported, is modest and should be tempered.

The prior-action memory and test-time augmentation use ground-truth previous actions at training time and model predictions with a memory buffer at test time; the contribution of temporal context vs. simply more compute/TTA could be more clearly disentangled, and dependence on ground-truth priors limits real-world deployment.

SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 partially relies on using 32 frames (58.3 -> 63.2) whereas the strongest baselines (TIM 56.4) typically use fewer frames; a frame-matched comparison would make the SOTA claim more convincing.

Training uses both official keys and narrations as augmentation, and the model is trained on the same validation distribution used for benchmark design decisions, raising mild concerns about leakage between method development and evaluation.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: fine-grained action understanding in video MLLMs, with a well-motivated benchmark (EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA) built via automatic hard-negative mining from specialist action recognition models rather than costly human curation.

Comprehensive evaluation: besides the new benchmark, results on four action recognition datasets (EPIC-KITCHENS-100, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30, MECCANO, Animal Kingdom), 13 general MLLM benchmarks, and multiple base models (LLaVA-Video-7B, LLaVA-OV-7B/0.5B, InternVL3-8B) demonstrate generality of the recipe.

Thoughtful experimental design: the IID vs. OOD distinction (AVION distractors for training, TIM for testing) with JSD statistics and agreement analysis, additive plus leave-one-out ablations, action-token design ablations, efficiency comparison of the two-stage pipeline (190x faster than multi-round scoring), and difficulty-level analysis.
Strong headline results (e.g., 34.8 -> 74.1 on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action recognition) and honest reporting that general benchmark gains are modest and not SOTA claims.
Good resource contribution: benchmark, data, code, and models are stated to be released; licensing information is provided.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity is not fully established: distractors come from TIM's top-K predictions without human verification. TIM's predictions can be actions actually occurring in the clip (false negatives), so some 'hard distractors' may be plausible or even correct answers, making the reported MLLM drops partly attributable to annotation noise. Human audit of a sample of MQAs would substantially strengthen the central claim that MLLMs 'struggle' with fine-grained actions.

Novelty is incremental: hard example mining (Shrivastava et al. 2016), a CLS-token-like auxiliary token, GPT-4o distillation, and choice-based fine-tuning are all existing ideas combined; the action-token ablation shows only ~3-4 points of the gain, most of which comes from data reformulation.

SOTA claims on action recognition rely on the two-stage pipeline that filters candidates using a specialist model (TIM top-20), which caps the achievable accuracy by the specialist and is not a purely 'generalist' comparison; the fair-comparison argument would be stronger with specialist-free structured prediction results reported prominently.

The GPT-4o comparison is limited to 8 frames ('cost-prohibitive' beyond), which disadvantages closed-source baselines on a video benchmark; the 21-point margin over GPT-4o may shrink with more frames.

Improvements on the 13 general MLLM benchmarks are small and mixed (several negative deltas, e.g., VideoDC, VideoChatGPT, NextQA), suggesting the gains are largely domain-specific to EPIC-KITCHENS-style egocentric cooking data; the impact beyond this niche could be limited.

Several design choices are empirically rather than analytically motivated (e.g., n=2 prior actions, 30% prior-action mix, delta=3s padding), and the attention-based analysis (Section 4.5) is correlational rather than causal evidence for the action token's mechanism.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: fine-grained action discrimination for video MLLMs is underexplored, and the hard-example-mining benchmark construction (using specialist model predictions as distractors) is an efficient and reproducible alternative to human or closed-source LLM curation.

Extensive empirical evaluation: EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA, four action recognition datasets, ten+ general video MLLM benchmarks, additive and leave-one-out ablations, difficulty-level analysis, and attention-based interpretability analysis.

Thoughtful OOD protocol: using AVION-generated distractors for training while testing with TIM-generated distractors, with supporting statistical analysis (JSD, overlap rates) to justify the IID/OOD split.

Practical contributions: the two-stage structured action pipeline (190x faster than multi-round appending), release of code/data/benchmark, and demonstration that the recipe transfers to other base models (InternVL3-8B, LLaVA-OV).
weaknesses: The headline 'SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100' claim is weakened by the evaluation design: LLaVAction is fine-tuned on in-domain EPIC-KITCHENS-100 training data and its candidate set is TIM's top-20 predictions, effectively making the MLLM a re-ranker of a specialist model. The comparison against prior work (many zero-shot or differently-trained) is not apples-to-apples, and the upper bound is capped by the specialist model. This ensemble-like setup should be stated more prominently.

The benchmark's test distribution is defined by TIM's predictions, and the IID setting (77.0) trains on TIM-generated distractors, i.e., essentially the test distribution. The OOD setting mitigates this, but the headline numbers risk overfitting to the distractor generator rather than measuring genuine fine-grained action understanding.

Contribution decomposition: the data reformulation (adversarial distractors) dominates gains; the action token adds only ~3.9 points and is an incremental design (a CLS-like token with auxiliary classification heads). The two-stage pipeline is also essentially a standard filter-then-choose scheme. Overall the methodological novelty is modest.

GPT-4o comparisons are limited to 8 frames ('cost-prohibitive'), and different frame counts are used across tables (8/16/32/64), making cross-table comparisons inconsistent and the GPT-4o comparison potentially unfavorable.

Ablation presentation is confusing: in Table 3, 'GPT-4o-based reformulation' appears twice with very different results (21.9 and 71.5), and the additive ordering is hard to follow; several per-component gains are within noise (e.g., temporal order learning 73.6 -> 73.4 before SAP).

The attention-based analysis (Section 4.5) is post-hoc, anecdotal (single qualitative clip), and the correlation metrics are not validated against ground truth; '99% of visual tokens exhibit lower correlations' is presented as evidence without significance testing.

Writing quality issues: multiple typos ('KITHCENS', 'limted', 'Snice', 'leave-on-out'), grammatical errors ('we proposed an action-related... regime' in present tense, 'adds negligible overhead'), and Equation 5 notation is informal. For a top-tier venue the manuscript needs a careful language pass.

Reproducibility claims are undercut by a missing URL ('available at' is truncated) and dependence on closed-source GPT-4o distillation for part of the training data; the exact mixture with LLaVA-Video-178K and its influence on general benchmark results is not fully ablated.
The difficulty-level analysis relies on GPT-4o to rate difficulty, introducing subjectivity that is not validated against human ratings.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap — fine-grained action discrimination in MLLMs — and demonstrates it convincingly with large performance drops for GPT-4o and strong open-source MLLMs when hard, model-generated distractors are used (Table 1).

The benchmark construction (EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA) is a useful community resource: automatic hard-example mining via specialist action recognition models is more scalable than human or closed-source LLM distractor generation, and the idea is generalizable to other action datasets (demonstrated on Meccano, Animal Kingdom, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30).

Careful experimental methodology: the IID vs. OOD distinction (training with AVION distractors, testing with TIM) explicitly guards against overfitting to the distractor generator's error distribution, supported by agreement statistics and JSD analysis in Appendix D. Additive and leave-one-out ablations (Tables 3, 11) isolate the contribution of each component.

Strong and broad empirical results: large gains on the new benchmark (34.8 → 74.1 OOD, 77.0 IID), SOTA on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action classification (58.3/63.2 vs. TIM's 56.4), improvements on three additional action recognition datasets, and consistent gains over the LLaVA-Video-7B baseline on 10 of 13 general video MLLM benchmarks.

Good reproducibility: code, data, benchmark, and models are released; training details, prompts, licenses, and many implementation specifics are documented; the appendix contains extensive qualitative and quantitative supporting material.

The action token ablation (Table 10), the structured-action-pipeline comparison with a 190x speedup over multi-round appending (Table 12), and the attention-based analysis add transparency to why the method works.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core ideas — hard example mining, multiple-choice reformulation, a CLS-like auxiliary token, and GPT-4o distillation for training data — are all established techniques applied in combination. The contribution is primarily an engineering/data contribution rather than a new method.

Circularity concern in the SOTA claims: LLaVAction's structured-action pipeline relies on TIM's top-K predictions at inference (K=20 for the main results), so the comparison with specialist models like TIM on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 is partly entangled with the very model being beaten. The benchmark itself is also built from TIM's errors, so distractor difficulty reflects one model's bias; the dependence of conclusions on this choice is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

The GPT-4o comparison is unfair: GPT-4o is evaluated with only 8 frames while LLaVAction uses up to 32-64 frames, and the authors note running GPT-4o beyond 8 frames is cost-prohibitive; the '21-point improvement over GPT-4o' headline claim should be interpreted cautiously.

Gains on general MLLM benchmarks (Table 7) are small and inconsistent (e.g., -0.4 on NextQA, -0.03 on VideoChatGPT, -0.1 on VideoDC), and the authors themselves note no improvement on VideoMME action recognition due to domain gap; general video understanding is only marginally affected.

Some inconsistency and presentation issues: Table 2 reports 71.7 (8f) for LLaVAction-LLaVA-Video-7B while the ablation Table 3 reports 74.1 (16f), which invites confusion; there are multiple typos ('EPIC-KITHCENS-100-MQA', 'limted', 'leave-on-out', 'Snice'), and Table 1 lacks error bars or significance tests for the comparisons between distractor sources.

The 'w/ action narration' setting (63.2) that produces the best EPIC-KITCHENS-100 result uses ground-truth clip narrations as candidate text, which may leak annotation phrasing in a way that the action-label setting does not; the implications of this choice for open-vocabulary applicability deserve more discussion.
